pages.text:
*Ama's Stall Ledger, Night 6. Bowls sold: 79. Weather: cold. Star anise: a handful. Which handful: unknown.*

I decided to be a scientist, at least for the next hour, because if this stall was going to survive, somebody had to understand how it actually worked. The mall was coming, the city was looking, and Ama had absolutely no notes.

I sat on a plastic stool right next to the great pot, my notebook open on my knee while the pencil stayed tucked behind my ear, just where it always was. I watched the steam curl up from the lid in slow, lazy loops.

Ama was wiping the counter with a rhythm I could almost hear, a steady thump-swish, thump-swish, and she just kept watching the pot without adding anything. I wrote down the time, 5:42 PM, then guessed the temperature was cold, and noted that the air smelled deeply of beef and soy. I was ready, patient, and for once, very still.

Ama stopped wiping and looked at me, then at the pot, before picking up the ladle.

"Yun-Lin," she said, "you are going to stand there all night?"

"I am observing," I said.

"Good," she said. "The soup needs a witness."
pages.image: A small girl in a green jacket sits on a plastic stool beside a large steaming metal pot, holding a notebook, watching a grandmother in a floral vest who holds a ladle and looks at the pot with a calm expression. All shop signs, banners and hanging boards are smooth plain solid-color cloth.

pages.text:
Ama lifted the lid, and the steam rushed out hot and heavy, filling the space between us before she even looked my way. She reached for a bowl on the counter and poured a dark stream into the pot. It hissed like an angry cat.

"Soy sauce," I said, scribbling it down.

"Until it is the right brown," Ama replied.

I wrote that down verbatim. That was not a measurement; that was a mood. She grabbed a chunk of ginger, roughly the size of my thumb, and dropped it in with a wet clatter.

"Ginger," I announced.

"This big," she said, holding up her hand to show me the scale.

I stared at her hand, broad and strong with short, clean fingernails, then I looked at the ginger, which was tiny. When I looked at her hand again, it seemed to be the size of a small shovel.

"A handful of star anise," she said, reaching for the jar.

She poured them into her palm, and it was a lot, more than I had expected. I wrote: HANDFUL (AMA'S). I tried to draw her hand, but it ended up looking like a claw.

"Salt?" I asked.

"Taste first," Ama said. "Talk later."
pages.image: Ama, a small sturdy grandmother with short silver curls and a flowery padded vest, holds out her open palm full of star anise pods to Lin, an eleven-year-old girl with a chin-length black bob and straight bangs, in a dark green padded jacket and a red-and-white checked apron, who holds a small notebook and looks on wide-eyed, a big pot steaming behind them at a night-market stall.

pages.text:
Ama ladled a small amount of broth into a paper cup and held it out to me. The steam hit my face, carrying the scent of deep, dark earth and sweetness.

I took a sip. It was hot and rich, but something was missing. It felt round, but not quite finished, like a song that stopped right before the last note.

"Salt?" I asked.

Ama shook her head. "Wait."

I waited, watching the steam rise off the cup. I tasted it again, this time closing my eyes. I let the flavor move around my mouth, searching for the edge of it.

"Still not," I said.

Ama reached into a jar on the shelf and pulled out a thin, dry curl of something orange. It looked like a piece of a dried leaf, and she dropped it into the pot.

"Try now," she said.

I sipped again, and my eyes opened wide. It was sharp and bright, cutting through the heavy beef flavor. It was exactly what was missing.

"How did you know?" I asked.

"My tongue told me," she said.

All shop signs, banners and hanging boards are smooth plain solid-color cloth.

pages.text:
Ama reached under the counter and pulled out a small cloth bag tied with red string. It looked like a pouch of sand, but it felt heavier in her hand.

"This goes in next," she said.

She untied the knot, and the smell hit me before the sight did. It was deep and warm, smelling exactly like the inside of a wooden cabinet in a house you used to visit in summer. I leaned in and sniffed hard. For a second, I forgot the stall, the mall, and the city review. I was just breathing.

"Mr. Tsai makes this," Ama said. "Every month. He lives by the temple."

She tipped the bag onto her palm, and eight things spilled out. Star anise, cinnamon bark, fennel seeds, Sichuan peppercorns, licorice root, tangerine peel, bay leaf, and clove.

I picked up a star anise. It had eight points, just like the sign on the market board. I looked at the others. They were all different, yet they fit together like pieces of a puzzle I had never seen before.

"Who is Mr. Tsai?" I asked.

"He knows things," Ama said. "About smells."

All shop signs, banners and hanging boards are smooth plain solid-color cloth.

pages.text:
Ama reached for the pot lid. Her right hand found the handle, but then it wobbled. It was a tiny shake, like a leaf trembling in a gust, but I saw it clearly. The steam swirled on the left side of the pot, but her fingers were on the right, where there was no vapor to blur her vision.

She lifted the lid anyway. Hot cloud poured out.

Ama did not look at her hand. She stared at the soup.

"Steam in my eyes," she said.

I watched her wrist. It stayed still as she set the lid back down and turned to wipe the counter. I looked at my notebook. I had listed the spices and drawn a diagram of the pot, but I had not written this part down. I pulled my pencil from behind my ear. In the bottom corner, in letters so small they looked like ants, I wrote: ASK MA.
pages.image: Ama, in her flowery vest, grips the lid of a big pot with a slight tremor while Lin, an eleven-year-old girl with a chin-length black bob and straight bangs, in a dark green padded jacket and a red-and-white checked apron, in the foreground looks down at her notebook with a serious, worried face.
